No it doesn't. It means she knows that she was ANNOYING them. That's not the same thing. Take the example of say, a smoker. You have a friend who smokes, and you don't smoke. You tell them every time you see them you mention that it's bad for them, and that they should quit. This annoys them. You realize this annoys them, but you really want them to quit for their own good, because you've seen the statistics, you know the science, and you don't want your friend to die prematurely. To them, you're insufferable, telling them what to do and how to live their life. To you, you're just trying to convince them of a plausible risk to their well being, but pragmatically eventually you stop because you realize that pressing the issue won't get them to stop, and you'll burn that bridge. You don't believe yourself to be in the wrong, after all, you don't want them to die or to become ill, but it's obviously annoying them for you to point it out to them regularly. Thus, someone who admits that the people around them find them insufferable do not necessarily believe themselves to be wrong for that. The same thing would apply to someone surrounded by smokers - Just because ALL of the people around you think you're insufferable because of it, doesn't necessarily mean you're wrong or that you think you're wrong. You're simply acknowledging that what you're doing is annoying them, but it could very well still be what you believe (and when these people are your friends and family and you're annoying them with it for a year, it's almost guaranteed to be what you believe, because after all you're risking burning bridges of all of your closest relations over ideology)
